title: MB1-03081
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal claimant (PC) and her three children are citizens of Jamaica. She is a 39 year old, single, high school graduate. The PC is the Designated Representatives for her two minor children. Her 19 year old son gave testimony on his own behalf. The claimants arrived in Canada in July 2008 and claimed for protection in May 2011. They are claiming protection because of membership in a particular social group under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). They are also claiming for protection because they are "persons in need of protection" and because their lives are at risk, and because they are at risk of cruel or unusual punishment under section 97 (1) (b) of the IRPA. The Chairperson's Guidelines on females fearing gender-related persecution were taken into account.

The hearing began as a show cause abandonment hearing. Counsel produced IRB documents showing that he and the claimants were advised that the hearing was scheduled for September 26, 2013, whereas, the file in my possession and my calendar showed it was scheduled for September 24. The cause for the discrepancy is unclear but counsel's documents clearly explain the absence. Counsel then requested a postponement as he was double-booked and had another matter in Family Court.

Counsel was referred to Rule 54. Counsel failed to ask for a postponement three days before the hearing, even though he stated that he had been aware of his double-booking for several weeks. None of the claimants are vulnerable persons. There is no emergency beyond the control of any of the parties. Counsel was informed that in accordance with rule 54, his request for postponement was denied. The hearing would proceed with him or without him. He agreed to stay. Counsel then raised a request to separate the claim of the 19 year old son from that of his mother and his siblings. The 19 year old stated that he was now an adult and that he had additional grounds for his claim. I noted that the claims remain based on similar questions of fact and law and that proceeding together better serves the efficient administration of justice. I further noted that the adult son of the PC could address his new grounds in his vive voce evidence and therefore there would be no injustice caused by keeping the claims joined. Thus in accordance with Rule 55, the motion to separate was denied. Counsel had no questions for the claimants at the hearing. Counsel indicated that he had not brought a copy of the Jamaica country binder to the hearing and would therefore be unable to provide a verbal submission today. He requested permission to provide a written submission. His request was granted and he was given one week, until 14:00 hrs, November 12, 2013, to provide his submission. As of the date of signing this decision no submissions were received from counsel nor did counsel make an application to extend the deadline for written submissions.

The PC requested she give her testimony without the presence of her adult son. She was told that, as an adult, he has the right to hear all her evidence. I then asked XXXX if he would waive that right and would step outside while his mother testified. He agreed to do so. The PC gave her evidence in the absence of her son. He gave his evidence before his mother and in her presence and then left the hearing room. SUMMARY OF ALLEGATIONS (from the principal claimant's PIF)
The PC is claiming for protection as a single mother and as a lesbian. In 1990 the PC discovered that she was intimately interested in a female schoolmate.

In 1991 the PC was sexually assaulted by members of a criminal gang. One of these members was XXXX XXXX. "We were beaten, raped , and sodomized. We were also insulted and threatened by the gang." This was considered normal activity in the PC's community. The PC had to take it and be quiet about it. She began a relationship with XXXX XXXX [the father of two of her children] .

XXXX still wanted the PC for himself. He started to spread rumours about her and he called her names, teased her, and verbally abused her in crowded places. In 1992 XXXX intensified his abuse. Late in 1992, XXXX beat the PC and stabbed her. She reported this to the Police and the constable told her if she told him where XXXX was, the police would arrest him as he was wanted for multiple shootings, rapes and murders. She left feeling helpless and scared.
The PC subsequently learned that the police had shot and killed XXXX and that "several members of his gang were captured and imprisoned."
Her son XXXX was attacked with guns several times because he refused to carry a gun.

In December 2007, the PC began a sexual relationship with a woman named XXXX XXXX. "On April XXXX, 2008, we were seen kissing in my home by someone who was peering through a hole in the door and an alarm was raised. We were beaten by three men (known only to us as XXXX, XXXX, and XXXX.)". The PC was hit in her face with a gun and kicked several times. She managed to run away. She then was able to get another Visa for Canada.
The claimants' identities are accepted on the basis on their genuine passports.

I find that the claimants are not "convention refugees" under s 96 of the IRPA. I further find that they are not "persons in need of protection" under s 97 of the IRPA. My reasons for these finding follow.
The determinative issue is credibility, and, in the alternative, state protection.

The PC testified that she feared being killed or beaten and abused by gang members if she had to return to Jamaica. She was asked when she first had such fears and she said that she has had them since April 2008. Given the numerous previous and rather horrific assaults related in her PIF, she was asked why she did not have such fears before 2008. She replied that she was able to cope OK until April 2008. Asked why she came to Canada in 2008, she said it was because of the "event" and that she was being hunted by gang members.

The PC was asked about the "event" of April 2008. She testified that a woman named XXXX caught the PC and XXXX "in a sexual manner". The PC was asked what did XXXX then do. The PC testified that XXXX did not say anything. She testified that XXXX ran away and the PC and XXXX also "ran off." She testified that she ran down the street and called her sister. The PC was asked to confirm that she was seen by XXXX and that at the time of the event she was not harmed. She confirmed those alleged facts.
The PC was asked where she and XXXX were located when caught by XXXX. She testified that they were indoors and that the PC saw XXXX outside by a window.

The PC was confronted with the contradiction between her testimony and her PIF narrative. In the latter, the PC wrote that XXXX saw them through a hole in the door. The PC then repeated that she saw XXXX at the window. Asked again to explain the contradiction, she said that she was not sure. This does not resolve the contradiction. Her credibility is tarnished.

The PC testified that she was not beaten on the day of the event but that the beating took place about a week later on XXXX April, 2008. The PC was confronted with this contradiction with her PIF in which she states that the discovery event happened on XXXX April 2008. The PC said that she was sure she was beaten on the XXXX. This does not resolve the contradiction. Her credibility is damaged.

The PC testified that she reported the April beating to the police and provided the police with the nicknames of the assailants - XXXX, XXXX, and XXXX. The PC was confronted with a contradiction with her PIF where she states the third assailant was XXXX not XXXX. She replied that she could not remember. This does not explain the contradiction since she affirmed that her PIF was complete, accurate, and truthful at the start of the hearing.

The PC was confronted with a contradiction between her PIF and her testimony. In her PIF an alarm was raised when she and her girlfriend were discovered, they were beaten at that time, and the PC managed to escape. In her testimony, she never mentioned an alarm being raised and testified that the beating was about a week after the discovery. She replied that she was beaten on the XXXX. This does not explain the several contradictions between her PIF and her testimony. Her credibility is eroded.

The PC testified that she went to the police two times to make complaints. I note this statement contradicts her six page, single space, typewritten, PIF narrative where the PC only states she was "forced to go to the police" by XXXX in 1992 at paragraph 23. Nowhere in the PIF does the PC say she went to the police following the "event" of April 2008. The PC was asked for copies of the police complaints and she did not have them.

The PC was asked if she had any letters from XXXX to corroborate the alleged relationship. She had none. She was asked if she had any documentary evidence to corroborate XXXX's alleged death. She had none. In the context of other credibility concerns, the lack of police reports, witnesses, affidavits or any other documentary evidence to corroborate her allegations, leads to another negative credibility inference.

The PC testified that she has been in Canada for five years. She was asked if she is currently in a lesbian relationship and she said no. She was asked if she has had a lesbian relationship since coming to Canada and she said yes. She was asked if she had affidavits from her former previous partner or partners in Canada to corroborate her allegation. She said no. Asked why not, the PC said she did not know that she would need such corroboration. The PC has retained professional counsel. Counsel attended the hearing. XXXX counsel would have known and would have advised his or her client to obtain as much corroboration, written or in person, to corroborate such a central allegation.

Her son testified that he was persecuted in Jamaica because his mother was gay. He was asked if, to his knowledge, how many gay relationships his mother, the PC, has had in Canada. He replied, "none that I know of."

Lesbians are not persecuted in Canada. Same sex relationships are legal and not simply tolerated. The evidence is that the PC has three children by two different men. Mindful of the IRB guidelines, it must be noted that while these facts do not refute that the PC is a gay woman, they do nothing to confirm it and can and do raise some reasonable doubt in my mind.
Based on the above, and in context of other credibility issues, I find that the PC, on a balance of probabilities, is not a gay woman. Her credibility is impaired in consequence.

The PC's exhibits include at pages 3/26 to 26/26 handwritten notes from staff at the Ottawa Rape Crisis Centre. Not all the pages/ comments are legible to me. I do make the following observations. First, I did not find any allegation that the PC is gay. Secondly, the PC was asked when she first sought out counselling given all the trauma she had endured in her country in Canada and she said it was in 2012, after she had filed for protection, i.e over four years after her arrival here. Thirdly, at page 26/26, the PC says that she was shot at during the April 2008 incident. She states that "she was friends with a woman and community members saw them kiss - these community members shot at her (while she and the kids were in the house), broke into their home, threatened their lives, ....". This story contradicts the PC's PIF narrative and her testimony at the hearing. No community members were alleged to have harmed her in either her PIF or testimony; it was three gang members. Nowhere did she mention in her PIF or testimony that shots were fired. Nowhere did she mention the presence of her children.

Waiting four years to seek counselling, after such traumatic events, is a behaviour inconsistent with the PC's alleged fears. Second, the fact that the PC only sought counselling and counselling documentary evidence after she had retained counsel and filed for protection, leads me to believe, in the context of other credibility concerns, that it was done simply to buttress her claim. For all these reasons, her credibility is reduced.
The contradictions between the PC's PIF narrative, her oral testimony, and what she told counsellors concerning what happened in April 2008 lead to a further negative credibility inference.

XXXX was asked why he feared going back to Jamaica. He said he fears that gunmen will kill him because his mother is gay. Asked if he was gay he said no. He was then asked why would gunmen kill him since he was not gay. He said they threatened and beat him repeatedly. Given an opportunity to introduce new grounds for a claim of protection, XXXX essentially relied on his mother's claim - she is gay therefore he is at risk. Given that I have concluded she is not credible, I find that his claim is not credible either.
Based on the above, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that these claimants are not credible. This finding alone is fatal to their claims. State protection

In the alternative, there is the issue of state protection. Did the PC seek the protection of her state and would state protection be available to this claimant should she return today to Jamaica? Jamaica is a democratic state. Thus, the presumption that state protection exists in Jamaica is very strong and the claimant is required to provide clear and convincing evidence to rebut that presumption.

As reflected by Comacho (FC 830 2007), " in the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim [...] at least where the state is a functioning democracy." Ignorance on the part of a claimant may explain why a claimant did not reasonably exhaust all potential sources of state redress and protection in a particular country, but it does nothing to rebut the presumption that adequate, if imperfect, state protection in a democratic state like Jamaica exists. Phrased differently and as stated in Kim (FC 1126 2005), a "subjective reluctance to engage the state" does not rebut the presumption of adequate state protection. As said in Ward, "clear and convincing confirmation of a state's inability to protect must be provided. For example, a claimant might advance testimony of similarly situated individuals let down by the state protection arrangement or the claimant's testimony of past personal incidents in which state protection did not materialize. Absent some evidence, the claim should fail, as nations should be presumed capable of protecting their citizens." The claimant did not provide clear and convincing proof rebutting the presumption of state protection in Jamaica; nor did she provide clear and convincing evidence of the inability of similarly situated individuals to access state protection.

In Kadenko v. Canada (Solicitor General) [1996], 143 D.L.R. (4th) 532, leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada refused on May 8, 1997, it stated that "the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all the courses of action open to him or her".

In 2011 FC 312, the court noted: "It is well established law that the threshold necessary to rebut the presumption of State protection is such that an applicant must take all necessary steps to avail itself of the assistance of the state. It has also been held that one refusal will not suffice to rebut the presumption of state protection (See Kadenko v MCI (1996), 143 DLR (4th) 532 at 534 FCA. Morales Lozada v MCI, 2008 FC 397 paras. 28 to 30. In reviewing the Board's decision in the present case I find it reasonable to find that the applicant had not taken all the necessary steps to obtain the assistance of the authorities..."

The objective documentary evidence on the adequacy of state protection in Jamaica is clearly mixed. This is particularly so in the context of domestic violence and protection to members of the Gay Men, Lesbians, Bisexual and Transgender (LGBT) community. The objective evidence shows that the state is active at the operational level in taking on the gangs and the claimant's own testimony reflects that fact.

According to the objective evidence1: "Jamaica is a constitutional parliamentary democracy. In December 2011, the opposition People's National Party (PNP) won 42 of the 63 seats in the House of Representatives, and PNP leader Portia Simpson Miller took office as prime minister on January 5. International election observers deemed the elections transparent, free, fair, and without violence. During the year there were instances in which elements of security forces acted independently of civilian control. The most serious human rights problems were alleged unlawful security force killings; cases involving the violation of rights that were not resolved in a timely way; poor prison and jail conditions, including abuse of detainees and prisoners; and incarceration of children with adults. Other human rights problems included an overburdened and ineffective judicial system and frequent lengthy delays in trials, violence against and sexual abuse of children, violence and discrimination against women, trafficking in persons, violence against persons based on their suspected sexual orientation, and vigilante justice meted out by violent mobs. The government took steps to investigate and punish members of the security forces who committed abuses, but in many instances a lack of witnesses and insufficient forensics equipment precluded arrests or prosecutions, thus providing the appearance of impunity for police who committed crimes [...]. Role of the Police and Security Apparatus The JCF has primary responsibility for internal security and is assisted by the Island Special Constabulary Force. The Jamaica Defence Force (JDF) has responsibility for national defense, maritime narcotics interdiction, and JCF support. The JDF routinely conducted joint patrols and checkpoints in conjunction with the JCF. In her capacity as minister of defense, the prime minister approves all JDF operations in support of the JCF. The Ministry of National Security exercises the prime minister's authority for oversight of the JCF and JDF. The JCF is headed by a commissioner who delegates authority through the ranks to constables. The force maintains divisions focusing on community policing, special response, intelligence gathering, and internal affairs. In 2010 the government created INDECOM to investigate actions by members of the security forces and other agents of the state that result in death or injury to persons or the abuse of the rights of persons. In April 2011 INDECOM replaced the JCF's Bureau of Special Investigations (BSI) as the lead investigator of incidents involving fatal shootings by police. INDECOM had 47 staff members, including 30 investigators, but cited lack of resources to perform forensic analysis and identification of security personnel involved in incidents as major obstacles faced in its investigations of police killings. The DPP issued its rulings on cases involving security forces on average 27 months after the final submission of files from the BSI or INDECOM. In 2011 INDECOM awaited rulings from the DPP on 40 cases. INDECOM also expressed concern that agents of the state concealed their identities in interactions with the public, including incidents of killings by security forces. According to JCF records, 192 police officers, or 48.5 percent of the 396 officers who took voluntary lie-detector tests during the year, did not pass or complete the test. The assistant police commissioner did not state whether the officers who failed would be disciplined in any way. However, during the year officials retired 15 officers and denied reenlistment to 27 officers for corruption or ethics reasons. In addition authorities dismissed nine officers for corruption, charged 43 other officers with corruption, and charged 45 citizens with corrupting JCF staff. The JFJ reported that at least 21 police officers responsible for fatal shootings in recent years had fled the country and were living abroad. The JFJ alleged that since it took the DPP so long to determine that police personnel should be charged with a crime, there was possible collusion between the accused police officers and their colleagues, allowing accused officers to escape. The JCF continued a community-policing initiative to address the long-standing antipathy between the security forces and many poor inner-city neighbourhoods. Through the Community Safety and Security Branch, during the year the JCF conducted targeted training of 2,735 officers, 778 of whom were deployed in 360 communities island wide. The branch trained community safety officers and assigned JCF personnel to targeted schools as resource officers to stem school violence. These officers also served as liaisons between the students, faculty, parents, and police. The government bolstered these efforts through public education and by nominating deputy divisional commanders with responsibility to introduce community policing to all the communities within their division. All JCF officers were required when possible to take a "graduated response" before using lethal force. Officers were also required to take an annual refresher course on the use of nonlethal equipment, but this did not always occur, due to a lack of funds and equipment [...]."

The PC was asked if the state would protect her if she went back to Jamaica and she said no. Asked why not, she said "no, you can't rely on them." She provided no objective evidence to support her reply.

The PC testified that she was unsatisfied with the police response when she made a complaint and that when she complained they treated her "like trash." She was asked if she made a complaint to the Jamaican Constabulary Force Centre for Investigations of Sexual offenses and Child Abuse and she said "no, I did not, because I got nothing the first time". She was asked if she sought help from a JCP "specialist officer on sexual violence" and she said no. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the PC did not exhaust all possible and reasonable sources of state protection , even within the JCF.

The PC was referred to paragraph 25 of her PIF narrative where she stated that the police shot and killed XXXX and captured and imprisoned members of his gang. She was asked if this is an example of the police doing their job and she said yes. The PC has shown a subjective reluctance to approach the state but her own testimony shows that the state takes effective and adequate measures against criminals and gang members. The PC did not adduce clear and convincing evidence that state protection would be inadequate should she return to her country. On the contrary, her evidence concerning the fate of XXXX is that her state is taking measures at the operational level to provide adequate state protection. The PC has failed to rebut a strong presumption of state protection in a democratic state such as Jamaica. This finding is alone fatal to these claims. In the circumstances of the case before me, the claimants have failed to provide clear and convincing evidence that their state would not provide them adequate protection should they return to Jamaica. That failure is alone fatal to their claims for refugee protection.

For all the above noted reasons, I find that the claimants are not "Convention refugees" nor are they "persons in need of protection." Consequently their claims for protection in Canada are denied. Alexander George Johnstone Alexander George Johnstone December 27, 2013 Date /el 1 Exhibit A-1: National Documentation Package on Jamaica, May 31, 2013.
